html:
In 1868 the new Meiji government of Japan ordered that Shinto be separated from Buddhism. The two had been woven together for about a thousand years, and the split was used to build a state religion around the emperor.

Before this, most shrines and temples shared grounds, priests and rites. Many kami, the Shinto gods, were treated as local forms of Buddhas. Buddhist monks often ran the shrines.

After the Meiji Restoration, leaders wanted to ground the emperor's authority in Shinto myth, going back to the Kojiki. Orders in 1868 told shrines to remove Buddhist statues, objects and priests. Buddhism was also tied to the fallen shogunate, which had used temples to register every household.

In many places a movement to "abolish Buddhism and destroy Shakyamuni" followed. Crowds and officials burned temples, smashed statues and melted bells, and many monks were forced back to lay life. The violence faded within a few years. State Shinto lasted until 1945; the next year the emperor's Humanity Declaration denied his divinity.
sum: In 1868 the new Meiji government of Japan ordered that Shinto be separated from Buddhism. The two had been woven together for about a thousand years, and the split was used to build a state religion around the emperor.
